In [[category theory]], a branch of mathematics, the '''density theorem''' states that every [[presheaf of sets]] is a [[Limit and colimit of presheaves|colimit]] of [[representable functor|representable presheaves]] in a canonical way.<ref>{{harvnb|Mac Lane|1998|loc=Ch III, § 7, Theorem 1.}}</ref>

For example, by definition, a [[simplicial set]] is a presheaf on the [[simplex category]] Δ and a representable simplicial set is exactly of the form <math>\Delta^n = \operatorname{Hom}(-, [n])</math> (called the standard ''n''-simplex) so the theorem says: for each simplicial set ''X'',
:<math>X \simeq \varinjlim \Delta^n</math>
where the colim runs over an index category determined by ''X''.

== Statement ==
Let ''F'' be a presheaf on a category ''C''; i.e., an object of the [[functor category]] <math>\widehat{C} = \mathbf{Fct}(C^\text{op}, \mathbf{Set})</math>. For an index category over which a colimit will run, let ''I'' be the [[category of elements]] of ''F'': it is the category where
# an object is a pair <math>(U, x)</math> consisting of an object ''U'' in ''C'' and an element <math>x \in F(U)</math>,
# a morphism <math>(U, x) \to (V, y)</math> consists of a morphism <math>u: U \to V</math> in ''C'' such that <math>(Fu)(y) = x.</math>
It comes with the [[forgetful functor]] <math>p: I \to C</math>.

Then ''F'' is the colimit of the [[diagram (category theory)|diagram]] (i.e., a functor)
:<math>I \overset{p}\to C \to \widehat{C}</math>
where the second arrow is the [[Yoneda embedding]]: <math>U \mapsto h_U = \operatorname{Hom}(-, U)</math>.

== Proof ==
Let ''f'' denote the above diagram. To show the colimit of ''f'' is ''F'', we need to show: for every presheaf ''G'' on ''C'', there is a natural [[bijection]]:

:<math>\operatorname{Hom}_{\widehat{C}} (F, G) \simeq \operatorname{Hom} (f, \Delta_G)</math>
where <math>\Delta_G</math> is the [[constant functor]] with value ''G'' and Hom on the right means the set of [[natural transformation]]s. This is because the [[universal property]] of a colimit amounts to saying <math>\varinjlim -</math> is the [[left adjoint]] to the [[diagonal functor]] <math>\Delta_{-}.</math>

For this end, let <math>\alpha: f \to \Delta_G</math> be a natural transformation. It is a family of morphisms indexed by the objects in ''I'':
:<math>\alpha_{U, x}: f(U, x) = h_U \to \Delta_G(U, x) = G</math>
that satisfies the property: for each morphism <math>(U, x) \to (V, y), u: U \to V</math> in ''I'', <math>\alpha_{V, y} \circ h_u = \alpha_{U, x}</math>
(since <math>f((U, x) \to (V, y)) = h_u.</math>)

The Yoneda lemma says there is a natural bijection <math>G(U) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}(h_U, G)</math>. Under this bijection, <math>\alpha_{U, x}</math> corresponds to a unique element <math>g_{U, x} \in G(U)</math>. We have:
:<math>(Gu)(g_{V, y}) = g_{U, x}</math>
because, according to the Yoneda lemma, <math>Gu: G(V) \to G(U)</math> corresponds to <math>- \circ h_u: \operatorname{Hom}(h_V, G) \to \operatorname{Hom}(h_U, G).</math>

Now, for each object ''U'' in ''C'', let <math>\theta_U: F(U) \to G(U)</math> be the function given by <math>\theta_U(x) = g_{U, x}</math>. This determines the natural transformation <math>\theta: F \to G</math>; indeed, for each morphism <math>(U, x) \to (V, y), u: U \to V</math> in ''I'', we have:
:<math>(G u \circ \theta_V)(y) = (Gu)(g_{V, y}) = g_{U, x} = (\theta_U \circ Fu)(y),</math>
since <math>(Fu)(y) = x</math>. Clearly, the construction <math>\alpha \mapsto \theta</math> is reversible. Hence, <math>\alpha \mapsto \theta</math> is the requisite natural bijection.
